problem.summary: Detection datasets are far smaller and more expensive to label than classification datasets, so detectors stay limited to a few hundred object categories; additionally the original YOLO suffers from localization errors and low recall relative to region-proposal methods.
statements: Most detection methods are constrained to a small set of objects because detection datasets are limited compared to classification datasets.
Labeling images for detection is far more expensive than labeling for classification or tagging.
YOLO makes a significant number of localization errors and has relatively low recall compared to region proposal-based methods.

evidence.quote: However, most detection methods are still constrained to a small set of objects.
labelling images for detection is far more expensive than labelling for classification or tagging
Error analysis of YOLO compared to Fast R-CNN shows that YOLO makes a significant number of localization errors.

background.summary: The work builds directly on the original YOLO detector, on anchor-box designs from Faster R-CNN, on multi-resolution feature maps in Faster R-CNN/SSD, and on WordNet/WordTree hierarchies for label structure.

relatedWork.name: YOLO
relatedWork.relation: the base detector that YOLOv2 improves
relatedWork.quote: YOLO suffers from a variety of shortcomings relative to state-of-the-art detection systems.

relatedWork.name: Faster R-CNN
relatedWork.relation: source of the anchor-box prior design that YOLOv2 adopts
relatedWork.quote: Instead of predicting coordinates directly Faster R-CNN predicts bounding boxes using hand-picked priors [15].

relatedWork.name: SSD
relatedWork.relation: prior multi-scale detector whose feature-map strategy informs the passthrough layer
relatedWork.quote: Faster R-CNN and SSD both run their proposal networks at various feature maps in the network to get a range of resolutions.

relatedWork.name: WordNet
relatedWork.relation: lexical resource used to build the WordTree label hierarchy
relatedWork.quote: ImageNet labels are pulled from WordNet, a language database that structures concepts and how they relate [12].

evidence.quote: The most common detection datasets contain thousands to hundreds of thousands of images with dozens to hundreds of tags [3] [10] [2].
Classification datasets have millions of images with tens or hundreds of thousands of categories

solution.summary: YOLOv2 upgrades YOLO with batch normalization, a high-resolution classifier, convolutional anchor boxes with k-means-derived priors, direct location prediction, a passthrough layer, multi-scale training and a new Darknet-19 backbone; YOLO9000 then jointly trains detection and classification over a WordTree hierarchy of 9000+ classes.
solution.approach: Improve a single-stage detector with a set of design changes and then train it jointly on detection and classification data whose labels are merged through a hierarchical WordTree.
components: Batch normalization on all convolutional layers
Fully convolutional YOLO with 5 anchor-box priors from k-means clustering
Direct location prediction with sigmoid-constrained grid-cell offsets
Passthrough layer concatenating 26x26 features into the 13x13 map
WordTree hierarchical label space and joint detection/classification loss

evidence.quote: Finally we propose a method to jointly train on object detection and classification.
We choose k = 5 as a good tradeoff between model complexity and high recall.
The network predicts 5 bounding boxes at each cell in the output feature map.
Our method uses a hierarchical view of object classification that allows us to combine distinct datasets together.

experiments.summary: YOLOv2 is evaluated on PASCAL VOC 2007/2012 and COCO with speed measured on a Titan X, while YOLO9000 is validated on the ImageNet detection task, where most test classes have only classification labels; ablations in Table 2 trace the gain from 63.4 to 78.6 VOC mAP.

evidence.quote: At 67 FPS, YOLOv2 gets 76.8 mAP on VOC 2007.
YOLOv2 achieves 73.4 mAP while running far faster than competing methods.
YOLO9000 gets 19.7 mAP overall with 16.0 mAP on the disjoint 156 object classes that it has never seen any labelled detection data for.

limitations.summary: Anchor boxes slightly reduced mAP despite higher recall, YOLO9000 has detection labels for only 44 of 200 ImageNet detection classes and struggles on clothing/equipment categories, and its comparison to prior detectors is confounded by different training data.
items: Switching to anchor boxes lowered intermediate mAP from 69.5 to 69.2 even though recall rose from 81% to 88%.
YOLO9000 only has labelled detection data for 44 of the 200 ImageNet detection classes.
The model struggles to learn categories such as clothing and equipment where COCO supplies no bounding-box labels.
Comparison against DPM is qualified because YOLO9000 is trained on different datasets with only partial supervision.

evidence.quote: Even though the mAP decreases, the increase in recall means that our model has more room to improve.
so YOLO9000 struggles to model categories like “sunglasses” or “swimming trunks”.
This mAP is higher than results achieved by DPM but YOLO9000 is trained on different datasets with only partial supervision [4].

futureDirections.direction: Apply the joint weakly-supervised technique to image segmentation.
futureDirections.quote: For future work we hope to use similar techniques for weakly supervised image segmentation.

futureDirections.direction: Improve detection by using stronger strategies for assigning weak labels to classification images during training.
futureDirections.quote: We also plan to improve our detection results using more powerful matching strategies for assigning weak labels to classification data during training.

futureDirections.direction: Use hierarchical classification for dataset combination in classification and segmentation.
futureDirections.quote: Dataset combination using hierarchical classification would be useful in the classification and segmentation domains.

futureDirections.direction: Bring different sources and structures of data together to build stronger visual models.
futureDirections.quote: We will continue looking for ways to bring different sources and structures of data together to make stronger models of the visual world.

applications.detail: Low-latency detection is required by robotics and self-driving applications.
applications.quote: Most applications for detection, like robotics or selfdriving cars, rely on low latency predictions.

applications.detail: At 288x288 the detector runs above 90 FPS, suitable for multiple video streams.
applications.quote: This makes it ideal for smaller GPUs, high framerate video, or multiple video streams.

applications.detail: YOLO9000 detects over 9000 object categories in real time.
applications.quote: YOLO9000 can detect a wide variety of object classes in real-time.

deploymentClaims: 67 FPS at 76.8 mAP and 40 FPS at 78.6 mAP on VOC 2007 (Geforce GTX Titan X).
At 288x288 input it runs at more than 90 FPS.
One trained model runs at multiple resolutions for a smooth speed/accuracy tradeoff.
Code and pre-trained models are released at pjreddie.com/yolo9000.

evidence.quote: At 40 FPS, YOLOv2 gets 78.6 mAP, outperforming state-of-the-art methods like Faster RCNN with ResNet and SSD while still running significantly faster.
All of our code and pre-trained models are available online at http://pjreddie.com/yolo9000/.
